note.explanation: Privacy laws set rules for how organisations handle personal information. They help protect it from misuse and unauthorized access. Data ethics guides people to collect, store, and use information fairly. Important principles include transparency, respect for privacy, consent, data minimization, security, and accountability.
note.checkAnswer: Privacy laws are government rules that protect personal information; data ethics means handling information fairly and responsibly.
note.simple: Privacy laws help keep your personal information safe. Data ethics means treating information and the people it belongs to fairly.
note.checkQuestion: Name two principles of data ethics.
note.title: Legal and Ethical Frameworks
steps: Ask for consent before collecting someone's data.
Collect only the data that is needed.
Keep the data secure from unauthorized access.
Use and share the data responsibly.
Take responsibility and act if something goes wrong.

rationales: This is correct because data minimization means collecting only the data needed.

options: Collecting someone's data only after they agree
Collecting data secretly

rationales: This is correct because consent means the person agrees before their information is collected.
This is incorrect because secret collection does not seek the person's agreement.
This is incorrect because sharing without explanation is not responsible or transparent.
This is incorrect because data should be used for its intended purpose.

options: Inform affected people after a data breach and take steps to fix the problem

rationales: This is correct because the section says to inform affected individuals and take steps to fix the problem.
This is incorrect because hiding a breach avoids taking responsibility.
This is incorrect because blaming affected people does not address the organisation's responsibility.

examTips: This section can be tested with short questions asking for the purpose of privacy laws or how they protect data.
A long question may ask you to explain data ethics and its principles. Define data ethics, then explain transparency, respect for privacy, and accountability separately.
For full marks, use key terms from your textbook, such as consent, unauthorized access, encryption, data minimization, and accountability where relevant.
When a question asks how data is handled responsibly, organize your answer around collecting, storing, and sharing information.

explain.title: Privacy laws
explain.body: Privacy laws are rules set by the government to protect our personal information. They require companies and organizations to handle data responsibly. If a company misuses your data, such as sharing it without permission, you have the right to take legal action.

explain.title: Unauthorized access
explain.body: Accessing someone's personal information without permission is illegal. Hacking an email or social media account is an example. Unauthorized access can lead to identity theft or fraud, so companies should use strong security measures such as encryption.

explain.title: Data ethics
explain.body: Data ethics is about doing the right thing when it comes to collecting, storing, and using information. Its principles include transparency, respect for privacy, and accountability.

explain.title: Responsible data handling
explain.body: Ask for consent before collecting data, collect only what is needed, keep data secure, and share it carefully. If something goes wrong, take responsibility; for example, inform affected people about a data breach and take steps to fix it.

mistakes: Do not confuse privacy laws with data ethics: laws are government rules, while data ethics guides responsible behaviour in handling data.
Do not say that consent is only needed when data is shared; the section says to get consent before collecting it.
Do not describe data minimization as collecting all available information; it means collecting only the data needed.
Do not forget to explain the named principles in a long answer instead of only listing them.
Do not suggest that encryption makes careless sharing acceptable; data must still be shared carefully and only when necessary.
